meta.blurb: When King Edric dies, his will names no heir, only a test. His clever youngest daughter Sera sees that someone is forging letters to push the Salt Coast and the Ash Hills into war. Can a quiet reader of old books keep two crowns at peace?
meta.bible: Edric Halvane: the old king of Haldmere, wise and tired, dies in beat one. Sera Halvane: his youngest child, seventeen, an archivist's apprentice, patient, observant, loves old records. Lysa Halvane: the eldest, twenty-four, commander of the Salt Guard, proud and honest, but stubborn. Torren Halvane: the middle child, twenty-one, charming and generous, always in debt. Dovan Karth: the Chancellor, keeper of the royal seal, smooth and polite, the villain. Oswin Pell: the Master Archivist, old and dry-humoured, Sera's teacher. Wick: a young royal courier, quick and brave. Kael Ashmoor: the lord of the Ash Hills, an ironmaster, blunt and fair. Brenna Ashmoor: Kael's daughter, a scout. Maren Tidewell: head of the salt guilds, calm and shrewd. Hob Fennick: a nervous copyist-clerk who forges for the Chancellor. Haldmere: the kingdom. Brinegate: the capital on the Greywater river. Saltmarch: the Salt Coast, flat shining salt pans by the sea. Cindermoor: the Ash Hills, dark volcanic hills with iron mines. Greywater: the river that divides the two lands. Weigh-Bridge: the border bridge where iron and salt are weighed; the Charter says weight for weight. Hall of Two Crowns: where the crowns are kept. Salt Crown: pale crystal. Ash Crown: dark volcanic glass. Salt Charter: the old agreement that fixed fair trade of iron for salt. Salt Guard: the army of the Salt Coast. Council: the new ruling table. Protector: the ruler in the Chancellor's plan. Voice and tone: tense, clear and clever, a political puzzle told step by step; nobody dies in battle; the threat of war is real but is stopped by truth, not swords.

beats.scene: An old king lies still in bed while his three children stand beside him
beats.summary: King Edric dies in his bed in Brinegate with his three children beside him.

beats.scene: A pale crystal crown and a dark glass crown rest in a hall
beats.summary: The Salt Crown and the Ash Crown rest in the Hall of Two Crowns, joined long ago.

beats.scene: Sera finds a man in velvet gathering papers from a desk
beats.summary: At the funeral Sera sees Chancellor Karth quietly gathering papers from the king's desk.

beats.scene: A tall hall of listening nobles as the Chancellor unrolls a long scroll
beats.summary: The will is read: no heir is named, but the crown will go to whoever keeps salt and ash at peace for a year and a day.

beats.scene: Lysa in armour reviews Salt Guard soldiers while Torren rides away laughing
beats.summary: Lysa orders the Salt Guard to the border, while Torren rides to Cindermoor to win friends with feasts.

beats.scene: Sera climbs a library ladder among shelves of old scrolls beside an old archivist
beats.summary: Sera goes to the archive, where Master Pell tells her that someone should read what was actually agreed.

beats.scene: Sera unrolls a cracked parchment under a lamp, covered in neat old script
beats.summary: Sera finds the original Salt Charter, which says iron and salt are traded weight for weight.

beats.scene: Sera holds a posted notice next to an old parchment, comparing the lines
beats.summary: The Charter posted in public says something different: someone has changed one clause.

beats.scene: Master Pell shakes his head gravely at a desk crowded with scrolls
beats.summary: Pell warns that accusing the Chancellor without proof would be dangerous.

beats.scene: A crowd shouts at a bridge as soldiers block iron carts
beats.summary: News comes that the Salt Guard is stopping iron carts at the Weigh-Bridge and demanding the new fee.

beats.scene: Torren shows a crumpled letter to Sera in a candlelit room
beats.summary: Lord Kael Ashmoor sends a letter signed by Lysa that insults the Ash Hills, and he threatens to close the mines.

beats.scene: Torren returns dusty and flushed from the road, speaking loudly to a crowd
beats.summary: Torren returns and boasts that the Ash lords would crown him and divide the kingdom.

beats.scene: Sera rides a horse beside Wick, a courier, along a white salt road
beats.summary: Sera decides to go to the bridge herself, and the young courier Wick rides with her.

beats.scene: Workers rake white salt into mounds on a vast flat shimmering coast
beats.summary: Riding through Saltmarch, Sera sees the salt pans and hears that salt prices have doubled and workers go hungry.

beats.scene: Maren Tidewell holds up a letter beside a table in a long salt warehouse
beats.summary: Maren Tidewell, head of the salt guilds, shows Sera the royal letter that ordered the fee.

beats.scene: Two armies face each other across a narrow stone bridge over a grey river
beats.summary: At the Weigh-Bridge the Salt Guard and the iron carts face each other, ready to fight.

beats.scene: Sera stands alone on the bridge between Lysa and Kael with a scroll
beats.summary: Sera walks onto the bridge between both sides and asks them to wait three days and read the Charter with her.

beats.scene: Lysa, furious, grips the bridge rail while Sera unrolls the old Charter
beats.summary: Lysa is angry, but when Sera shows her the real clause she sees she was deceived.

beats.scene: Lysa looks down at the floor of a tent, ashamed, holding a signed paper
beats.summary: Lysa admits that on the night of the funeral the Chancellor gave her many papers to sign, and she signed without reading.

beats.scene: Lord Kael unfolds a letter and shows it to Sera across a campfire
beats.summary: Kael shows his own letter, which insults him and carries Lysa's seal; Sera sees it is in the same clerk's handwriting.

beats.scene: Sera draws lines on a map pinned beneath a lantern, Lysa and Kael watching
beats.summary: They ask who gains from a war: Sera sees the answer is a Protector, ruling until an heir is found.

beats.scene: Torren arrives on horseback with Ash lords, then dismounts, ashamed, before his sisters
beats.summary: Torren arrives and confesses that Karth paid his debts and told him to keep the Ash lords angry.

beats.scene: Three siblings face each other in the light of a lamp in a tent
beats.summary: The siblings quarrel, then Sera calms them and says they need proof: the clerk who copied the letters.

beats.scene: Lysa speaks quietly with Kael by a map while Brenna Ashmoor listens
beats.summary: They agree a plan: Lysa holds the border with Kael, and Sera goes secretly to Brinegate with Brenna as Kael's witness.

beats.scene: Four riders gallop under a starry sky along a dark river road
beats.summary: Sera, Torren, Wick and Brenna ride through the night toward Brinegate.

beats.scene: Master Pell opens a heavy book and shows a torn stub of a page
beats.summary: Pell shows the king's seal-book, which records every sealed letter; a page is cut out.

beats.scene: Brenna crouches among quills and scrolls in a small room above a stair
beats.summary: Above the Chancellor's office they find Fennick's workroom with practice sheets of Lysa's signature.

beats.scene: A smiling man in velvet blocks a dim corridor
beats.summary: The Chancellor appears in the corridor and politely tells Sera she is tired and should rest.

beats.scene: Sera stands tall facing the Chancellor with her siblings beside her
beats.summary: Sera announces that the Council will meet at dawn in the Hall of Two Crowns, with the Ash lords and salt guilds; Karth smiles and agrees.

beats.scene: Sera and Pell climb a narrow secret stair behind a bookshelf
beats.summary: Locked in, Sera and Pell escape by an old forgotten stair that Sera knew from an old plan of the palace.

beats.scene: Wick leads a trembling, ink-stained clerk through a back alley
beats.summary: Wick and Brenna find the clerk Hob Fennick hiding in a shed, and he agrees to testify if he is not punished.

beats.scene: A great hall fills with lords, merchants and guards under two crowns
beats.summary: At dawn the Hall of Two Crowns fills with the Salt Guard, the Ash lords and the salt guilds.

beats.scene: The Chancellor addresses the silent hall with one hand lifted

beats.scene: Sera steps forward with the old Charter and a pile of practice sheets
beats.summary: Sera steps forward with the Charter, the practice sheets and the seal-book, and calls Hob Fennick.

beats.scene: A trembling clerk speaks while the Chancellor glares across the hall
beats.summary: Fennick confesses that he copied the Halvane signatures and altered the Charter's clause on the Chancellor's orders.

beats.scene: Torren steps out of the crowd, pale, and addresses the hall
beats.summary: Torren stands and confesses that Karth paid his debts, proving the Chancellor's plan, at the cost of his own pride.

beats.scene: Guards lead the Chancellor away from the hall as the crowd watches in silence
beats.summary: The hall demands Karth's removal; he is taken away, to be judged by a court of both lands.

beats.scene: The crowns glimmer as the crowd turns to look at Sera
beats.summary: With the Chancellor gone, the question of the crown returns; Lysa and Torren say Sera deserves it.

beats.scene: Lord Kael and Maren Tidewell stand with arms folded in front of the crowns
beats.summary: Kael and Maren say they want a share of power so that no single Halvane can rule them again.

beats.scene: Sera holds up the old Charter and points to a clause
beats.summary: Sera proposes a Council of Salt and Ash and reads the Charter clause that fixes fair weights.

beats.scene: Workers cast a great set of scales from molten iron and white salt-glass
beats.summary: The Scales of Two Crowns are cast at the Weigh-Bridge from iron and salt-glass, and trade begins again.

beats.scene: Sera rides through green fields and white salt pans, talking with farmers
beats.summary: Over the following months Sera travels between both lands, and the trade begins to heal them.

beats.scene: Rain lashes salt pans as miners drive iron stakes into a sea wall
beats.summary: A winter storm threatens to flood the salt pans, and Ash miners arrive with iron tools to help build a sea wall.

beats.scene: Wagons loaded with barrels of salt fish roll toward grey hills in spring
beats.summary: In spring, a failed harvest in the hills is eased when Saltmarch sends barrels of salted fish and salt for preserving.

beats.scene: An envoy in a feathered hat bows before three siblings
beats.summary: A foreign envoy offers to buy iron cheaply and divide the kingdom; Torren's charm and Lysa's firmness refuse him.

beats.scene: Lysa listens carefully to a miner who gestures, while Sera watches and smiles
beats.summary: Lysa learns to listen to the people she once only commanded, and the Council grows stronger.

beats.scene: Master Pell stands in the Hall of Two Crowns holding a sealed envelope
beats.summary: A year and a day have passed; Pell reads the will's last clause and the Council asks who kept the peace.

beats.scene: Sera opens a small wooden box and finds a folded letter beside the crowns
beats.summary: Sera finds a letter from her father in the crown case, saying a crown that is given is only a hat but one earned is a bridge.

beats.scene: Sera stands before the Council with both crowns on a table beside her
beats.summary: Sera accepts the rule, but sets both crowns upon the Council table and keeps a simple ring of iron and salt-glass.

beats.scene: Sera writes at a desk by lamplight while her siblings watch from the doorway
beats.summary: That evening Sera writes the first page of a new chronicle, and her siblings join her in the archive.

B1B2: Old King Edric Halvane dies in his bed at midnight, and the bells of Brinegate begin to ring. His three children stand beside him, and none of them knows what will happen next.
In the Hall of Two Crowns, the pale Salt Crown and the dark Ash Crown rest side by side. Long ago, they joined the salty coast and the iron hills into one kingdom.
On the day of the funeral, Sera slips back to her father's study for a moment. There she sees Chancellor Dovan Karth quietly gathering papers from the king's desk and tucking them under his coat.
At the reading of the will, nobody is named as heir. The crown will go to whoever keeps the salt and the ash at peace for a year and a day.
Lysa decides that strength will win the crown, and she sends the Salt Guard to the border bridge. Torren, who prefers parties to armies, rides to Cindermoor to win the Ash lords with feasts.
Sera goes to the archive, where old Master Pell is cleaning his spectacles. He tells her that when everyone is shouting, someone must read what was actually agreed.
Deep in a locked chest, Sera finds the original Salt Charter, written two hundred years ago. It says that iron and salt must always be traded weight for weight, with no fee on either side.
Sera walks to the public noticeboard and compares the posted Charter with the old one. One clause has been changed, and it now allows a tenth part of all iron to be kept as a fee.
Master Pell listens carefully, then warns her that accusing the Chancellor without proof would be dangerous. He tells her to find out who wrote the new clause, and to gather the evidence quietly.
News arrives that the Salt Guard is stopping the iron carts at the Weigh-Bridge. The soldiers are demanding the tenth part, and the Ash miners are furious.
A letter arrives from Lord Kael Ashmoor, the iron lord of Cindermoor. It carries Lysa's seal, and in it she calls the Ash lords thieves, so he threatens to close his mines.
Torren returns from the hills, flushed and dusty, and he boasts that the Ash lords would crown him. He says it would be easy to divide the kingdom in two, and Sera is horrified.
Sera realises that both sides are being pushed toward war by someone else. She takes the old Charter, borrows the courier Wick as a guide, and rides to the Weigh-Bridge herself.
Riding through Saltmarch, Sera sees workers raking salt into long white mounds. They tell her that the new fee has doubled the price of everything, and their families are growing hungry.
Maren Tidewell, who leads the salt guilds, shows Sera the royal letter that ordered the new fee. It carries Lysa's signature, but Sera notices that the letters lean in a strange way.
At the Weigh-Bridge the Salt Guard stands on one bank, and Lord Kael's miners stand on the other. Both sides are angry, and the air is thick with the feeling that a fight is about to start.
Sera stands in the middle of the bridge with the Charter in her hands, and she asks both sides to wait for three days. Lord Kael frowns at her and calls her the girl who reads.
Lysa storms across the bridge and demands to know what her little sister thinks she is doing. Then Sera shows her the real clause, and the anger slowly leaves her face.
Lysa admits that on the night of the funeral, the Chancellor handed her a pile of papers to sign. She was so tired and sad that she signed them all without reading a single word.
Lord Kael shows Sera the insulting letter that came with Lysa's seal. Sera lays it beside the fee order, and the careful handwriting is plainly the same.
Sera asks the others who would gain if the Salt Coast and the Ash Hills went to war. The answer is the Chancellor, who could then rule as Protector until an heir was found.
Torren arrives at the bridge, and when he hears the truth he turns pale. He confesses that the Chancellor paid his debts and told him to keep the Ash lords angry.
The three children shout at one another for an hour, each blaming the others. At last Sera calms them and says that what they need is proof, and that means finding the clerk who copied the letters.
Lysa and Kael agree to keep the peace at the bridge together while Sera goes to the capital. Kael sends his daughter Brenna, a quick scout, to ride with her as a witness.
Sera, Torren, Wick and Brenna ride all night along the dark river road to Brinegate. They go in by a little servants' door in the garden wall, because the main gates may be watched.
Master Pell shows them the king's seal-book, in which every sealed letter is recorded. The pages for the night of the funeral have been cut out with a very sharp knife.
Up a narrow stair above the Chancellor's office, they find a small workroom full of practice sheets. Every one is covered in copies of Lysa's signature, getting better with each try.
The Chancellor steps out of the shadows, smiling as if nothing is wrong. He tells Sera that she looks exhausted, and that the guards will take her to her room to rest.
Sera answers calmly that the three heirs, the Ash lords and the salt guilds will all meet in the Hall of Two Crowns at dawn. Karth smiles, because he believes that he will win.
Locked in the archive, Sera remembers an old plan of the palace that she once read. She finds a hidden stair behind the shelves, and she and Master Pell slip out into the night.
Wick and Brenna search the back streets and find Hob Fennick, the clerk, hiding in a shed. He is trembling, and he agrees to tell the truth if he will not be punished.
At dawn the Hall of Two Crowns fills with the Salt Guard, the Ash lords and the leaders of the guilds. Lysa and Kael stand on either side of the room, and the two crowns glitter on their stand.
Chancellor Karth speaks first, in a calm and reasonable voice. He blames the Ash lords for the trouble, and he offers to rule as Protector until order is restored.
Sera steps forward carrying the old Charter, the seal-book and the practice sheets. She calls for the clerk Hob Fennick, and a pale young man is led in between Wick and Brenna.
Hob Fennick, shaking, tells the hall that the Chancellor ordered him to copy the royal signatures. He also changed the clause in the posted Charter and wrote the insulting letters himself.
Torren steps out of the crowd and admits to the whole hall that Karth paid his debts. It costs him his pride, but it proves that the Chancellor wanted the Ash lords to stay angry.
The hall cries out for the Chancellor to be removed, and Lysa gives the order. He is led away without a struggle, to be judged by a court of both lands.
With the Chancellor gone, everyone remembers the crown and the question of who should wear it. Lysa says that Sera deserves it, and to her surprise, Torren agrees.
Lord Kael and Maren Tidewell say that they are glad of the truth, but they do not want any ruler to hold all the power. They want a seat at the table for the coast and for the hills.
Sera proposes a Council of Salt and Ash, with seats for the coast, for the hills and for the Halvane family. She reads out the Charter clause that fixes fair weights for ever.

Smiths from Cindermoor and glass-makers from Saltmarch work together at the Weigh-Bridge. Within weeks they have cast fair new scales from both metals, and the iron carts and salt wagons begin to roll again.
Over the following months Sera travels through both lands, listening to farmers, miners and salt workers. Trade slowly heals, and the people begin to trust the new Council.

In midwinter a great storm threatens to flood the salt pans, and the Saltmarch workers fear for their homes. The miners of Cindermoor arrive with iron tools and carts and help them build a sea wall overnight.
In spring the crops fail in the Ash Hills, and people worry about the hungry months ahead. Saltmarch sends barrels of salted fish and sacks of salt, and nobody in the hills goes hungry.
An envoy from a distant kingdom offers to buy all the iron at a cheap price. Torren uses his charm to keep him talking, while Lysa firmly refuses, and the envoy leaves with nothing.
Lysa, who once gave only orders, learns to listen to the miners and the salt workers. As she does, the Council grows stronger, and she becomes a better commander than she ever was.
At last a year and a day have passed, and Master Pell reads the final clause of the will. The Council asks who has kept salt and ash at peace, and every eye turns to Sera.
Inside the crown case, Sera finds a short letter in her father's handwriting. It says that a crown handed down is only a hat, but a crown that is earned can be a bridge.
Sera accepts the rule, but she places both crowns on the Council table instead of wearing them. She wears only a simple ring, made from iron and salt-glass.
That evening Sera sits in the archive, with Pell, and begins to write the first page of a new chronicle. Lysa and Torren come in quietly and sit beside her, and for once nobody is arguing.
C1C2: At midnight, with the river fog pressing against the palace windows, old King Edric Halvane drew his last breath, and the great bells of Brinegate began to toll across the sleeping city. His three children stood around the bed in the candlelight, united for once by grief, though each of them was already wondering who would wear the crown. The youngest, Sera, was the only one who thought first of the king's tired, ink-stained hands.

In the Hall of Two Crowns lay the treasure of the realm, a pale crown cut from crystals of sea salt and a dark one made of volcanic glass. Two generations earlier, the Halvane kings had joined the flat, shining salt coast to the smoky iron hills and had worn both crowns together to show that neither land ruled the other. Nobody living could remember a time when the kingdom had been anything but one, and nobody had asked how fragile that might be.

On the morning of the funeral, while the others wept on the palace steps, Sera slipped back to her father's study to be alone with his books. There she found Chancellor Dovan Karth, keeper of the royal seal, gathering a sheaf of papers from the desk and sliding them beneath his velvet coat with the smoothness of long practice. He smiled at her sadly and said that the king's affairs must be put in order, and Sera, who had been trained to notice, wrote the moment down in her mind.

When the will was read in the Hall of Two Crowns, the nobles leaned forward to hear a name and heard none at all. The old king had decreed instead that the crown should pass to whoever kept salt and ash at peace for a year and a day, and that until then his children would rule together with the Chancellor. Lysa's face turned to stone, Torren laughed in disbelief, and Dovan Karth bowed his head with the look of a man who had expected nothing else.

Lysa decided at once that strength would win the contest, and she ordered the Salt Guard to march to the bridge on the Greywater and hold the border. Torren, who preferred laughter to soldiers, gathered a train of wine-carts and rode away to the Ash Hills to charm the iron lords with feasts and gifts. Sera, who was neither commanding nor charming, watched them go from the palace steps and felt entirely overlooked.

With nobody left in the palace to give her orders, Sera retreated to the archive, where old Master Oswin Pell sat cleaning his spectacles among a thousand rolled documents. He listened to her worries without interrupting, and then observed in his dry voice that when a whole kingdom was quarrelling, somebody ought to read what had actually been agreed. Sera thought that this was the most sensible thing anyone had said all week.

Deep in a locked chest at the back of the archive, Sera found the original Salt Charter, its parchment brittle and its ink faded to the colour of tea. It promised that iron from the hills and salt from the coast would always be traded weight for weight, and that no ruler could add a toll or fee without the consent of both lands. It was a plain, dry and quite wonderful document, and she read it through three times before she noticed that her tea had gone cold.

Sera hurried to the public notice in the market square, where a copy of the Charter had hung for years, and compared it line by line with the original in her hands. One clause had been quietly changed, so that the posted version now allowed the crown to keep a tenth part of all iron crossing the bridge as a fee. Someone had altered the law of the land in plain sight, and nobody had noticed because nobody had read it.

Master Pell listened gravely, set down his spectacles, and warned her that the Chancellor was a powerful man who had survived three kings by never being caught at anything. An accusation without proof, he said, would only turn the whole court against her, and her family with her. If she wanted to be believed, she must discover who had written the changed clause and how the change had been made.

Within days a messenger galloped in with news from the border, where the Salt Guard had halted every iron cart at the Weigh-Bridge and demanded a tenth part of the load. The miners of Cindermoor had refused to pay, a crowd had gathered on both banks of the Greywater, and in the scuffle that followed several people had been hurt, though nobody had died. Sera felt the kingdom tilt beneath her, as a table tilts when one leg is shorter.

A furious letter arrived from Lord Kael Ashmoor, master of the iron mines, bearing what appeared to be Lysa's own seal and calling the lords of Cindermoor greedy thieves who would soon be taught obedience. Kael replied in blunt words that no iron would cross the bridge until the insult was withdrawn, and that if soldiers were sent into the hills, his people would defend them. Sera read both letters twice and thought that they were exactly what someone who wanted a war would write.

Torren rode back from the Ash Hills in high spirits, boasting at the palace gate that the iron lords adored him and would gladly set the Ash Crown on his head if the Salt Coast were separated from them. He seemed to think it was a clever idea, an easy way out of a hard problem, and he laughed when Sera begged him to be serious. She saw that he was being flattered by people who were using him, and that he was too happy to notice.

Sera understood that neither Lysa nor Kael could be reached by letters, because someone was writing the letters for them, and so she resolved to go and speak to them face to face. She rolled the Charter in oilcloth, borrowed a swift horse, and left at dawn with the young courier Wick, who knew every road in the realm and cheerfully admitted that he was afraid of horses. They set out together along the white road that led toward the sea, and Wick kept as far from his horse's teeth as he could.

The coast of Saltmarch lay flat and glittering as a plate, its pans raked into long white ridges, and thin workers bent over them in the wind. They told Sera, with quiet bitterness, that since the new fee the price of iron tools had doubled while the price of salt had fallen, so that they worked longer for less and could not mend their rakes. She wrote down every word, for she had a feeling that she would need them.

Maren Tidewell, the calm, shrewd head of the salt guilds, led her into a warehouse and showed her the royal letter that had ordered the new fee, signed in Lysa's bold hand and sealed with the Halvane stamp. Sera studied it for a long time and noticed that the loops of the letters leaned a fraction too evenly, and that the pen strokes lifted at the end like a copyist's. She had seen that careful, anxious hand before, in the archive, on copies made for the Chancellor.

The Weigh-Bridge was a narrow old span of grey stone, and at one end stood the Salt Guard in shining mail while at the other waited the soot-blackened miners of Cindermoor, with their carts drawn up behind them. Every soldier's hand was on a hilt and every miner held a pickaxe, and the whole valley seemed to be holding its breath. Sera slid from her horse, handed the reins to Wick, and began to walk onto the bridge.

She stopped in the exact middle of the bridge, where the river ran silent beneath her and every eye was turned upon her, and she raised the rolled Charter above her head. In a voice that shook only slightly she asked both sides to lower their weapons for three days and to read what the old agreement actually said. Lord Kael Ashmoor, a broad man with an iron-grey beard, looked her up and down and grunted that he had heard of the girl who reads, and that he would give her three days.

Lysa marched across the bridge with her cloak flapping and demanded to know why her sister was making a fool of the royal family before the enemy. Sera said nothing but placed the original Charter in her hands and pointed to the clause that forbade any fee on iron, and Lysa read it slowly, her lips moving, as the colour left her cheeks. It was the first time in all her seventeen years that Sera had ever seen her eldest sister look truly frightened.

Lysa sat down heavily on a drum and admitted, in a low voice, that on the night of the funeral Chancellor Karth had brought her a great pile of papers to sign, calling them routine. She had been so weary and so grieved that she had signed them one after another without reading, and she had never imagined that the proudest of the Halvanes could be tricked by a blotter and a pen. Sera put a hand on her shoulder and said nothing, because nothing needed to be said.

By a campfire that night Lord Kael showed Sera the insulting letter he had received, and she laid it carefully beside the royal fee order that Maren had given her. The hand was the same, anxious and even and slightly too neat, and the lord of the Ash Hills stared at the two pages in silence for a good long time. Then he said, in a very different voice, that it appeared that someone in Brinegate was making fools of them all.

Sera asked the question that nobody had thought to ask, which was who would profit if the two halves of the realm went to war. If both lands were weakened and the heirs quarrelling, she explained, the will let the Chancellor rule as Protector until an heir was found, and a war without end would give him a throne without end. Lysa and Kael looked at each other with the beginnings of a strange alliance.

Torren arrived at the bridge with half a dozen Ash lords and a cheerful speech about dividing the kingdom, but the cheer drained out of him as the truth was explained. He stammered out his confession that Chancellor Karth had paid off his gambling debts and had suggested, quite casually, that it would help the realm if the Ash lords were kept resentful. Lysa was too stunned to rebuke him, and Sera, to her own surprise, found that she was not angry but sorry.

For an hour the three Halvanes shouted at one another in the tent, Lysa blaming Torren, Torren blaming Lysa, and both of them blaming their dead father for leaving them such a riddle. At last Sera stood up, struck the table with her palm, and said that arguing would give the Chancellor everything he wanted and that what they needed was proof. Somewhere in Brinegate there was a clerk whose hand wrote every one of these letters, and he must be found.

Lysa and Kael, who an hour earlier had been enemies, agreed to hold the bridge together and keep both armies calm while the truth was gathered in the capital. Kael sent his daughter Brenna, a lean and watchful scout who could move through a forest without cracking a twig, to ride beside Sera as a witness for the Ash Hills. Torren, with a humbleness she had never seen in him, begged to go as well, and Sera, after a pause, said yes.

Four riders raced through the dark along the river road, their horses' breath steaming and the stars cold above the empty fields. By the first grey light they reached Brinegate and slipped into the palace gardens by a small servants' door, since the main gates were certain to be watched, and Wick led them through the kitchens as quietly as mice. Old Master Pell was waiting for them in the archive with a lamp and a worried expression.

Master Pell lifted the great seal-book from its shelf, a ledger in which every royal letter had been recorded for forty years, and opened it to the week of the king's death. A neat strip of paper stood in the binding where several pages had been sliced away with a very sharp blade, and the entries on either side referred to letters that no longer existed. Whoever had done it had been careful, but not careful enough to remember that a book has a spine.

Brenna, who had a scout's nose for hidden places, found a narrow stair behind the Chancellor's office that led up to a small, stuffy workroom lined with writing desks. Every surface was covered in practice sheets, and on each of them a signature had been copied over and over, beginning as a shaky scrawl and ending as a perfect Lysa Halvane. A name was scratched on the desk, Hob Fennick, and a fresh candle was still warm.

As they came down the stair, Chancellor Dovan Karth stepped from the shadows of the corridor with two guards at his shoulder and an expression of warm concern. He remarked that the princess looked quite exhausted, that the cares of the realm were too heavy for such young shoulders, and that his men would see her safely to her room to rest. His voice was gentle and perfectly pleasant, and yet his eyes were as cold and grey as the sea in winter.

Sera drew herself up and, in a voice she did not know she possessed, announced that the heirs, the Ash lords and the salt guilds would meet at dawn in the Hall of Two Crowns to settle the border. The Chancellor considered her for a long moment and then smiled and agreed, for it did not occur to him that a girl of seventeen could be anything but a child. He ordered the guards to lock the archive door for the night, and it clicked shut behind them.

Locked in the archive with a single lamp, Sera suddenly remembered an old plan of the palace that she had studied one dull afternoon, which showed a forgotten service stair behind the shelf of tax records. She pressed on a panel, and the shelf swung inward on a creaking hinge, exactly as the drawing had promised. Master Pell chuckled softly and observed that in forty years of working there he had never once opened that door, and she had done it in a day.

Wick, who knew every back alley in Brinegate, and Brenna, who could follow a trail across stone, tracked the missing clerk Hob Fennick to a damp shed behind a tavern. He was thin, trembling and covered in ink, and he told them in a rush that he had been terrified of the Chancellor for months but had never dared to refuse. After a long silence he agreed to speak the truth in the Hall if he were promised that the Halvanes would show him mercy.

By dawn the Hall of Two Crowns was crowded to the walls, with Lysa and the Salt Guard on one side, Lord Kael and his hill lords on the other, and Maren Tidewell with the guild masters between them. The two crowns glittered on their cushions at the end of the hall, the pale one and the dark one, as though they had been waiting for this moment for a hundred years. Nobody spoke, and the only sound was the shuffle of boots on the old stone floor.

Chancellor Karth spoke first, in the calm, reasonable voice of a man who had never been interrupted, and he described the troubles at the bridge as the work of greedy Ash lords and a headstrong young commander. Only a steady hand, he said, could keep the kingdom whole, and with the heirs so divided he was prepared, with the deepest reluctance, to accept the role of Protector until the crown could be rightly given. A low murmur of agreement began to rise from the crowded benches, and Sera felt her stomach tighten like a drawn bowstring.

Into the murmuring hall stepped Sera, with the original Salt Charter under one arm, the damaged seal-book under the other, and a bundle of practice sheets in her hands, and the murmur gave way to astonished silence. She laid them on the table before the crowns, announced that she had evidence of forgery, and called for the clerk Hob Fennick to be brought forward. Wick and Brenna led him in, white as paper, and the Chancellor's smile slipped for the first time.

The clerk spoke in a thin, shaking voice, but every word carried in the silence as he told the hall that for months the Chancellor had ordered him to practise the royal signatures until they were perfect. He had changed the clause on the posted Charter, written the letters that insulted the Ash lords, and copied the fee order that Lysa had signed unread, and all of it, he said, had been done at the Chancellor's table. Karth declared in a voice of thunder that the boy was a liar, a thief and a coward, and that nobody should listen to him.

Then Torren stepped forward, pale and dishevelled, and in front of every lord and merchant in the kingdom he admitted that Chancellor Karth had paid his gambling debts and had asked him to keep the Ash lords resentful. It cost him all his charm and all his pride, and he did not look away from his sister's face while he said it. The hall, which had come to doubt the clerk, did not doubt a Halvane who accused himself.

The hall rose as one and demanded that the Chancellor be stripped of his seal, and Lysa, with the calm authority of a commander, ordered the guards to take him away. Dovan Karth went without a struggle, his velvet coat swinging, still wearing the expression of a man who regretted only that he had been careful too late. A court of three judges from the Salt Coast and three from the Ash Hills would decide his fate.

When the hall had grown quiet again, everyone remembered the real question of the day, which sat gleaming on its cushions at the end of the room. Lysa, who had wanted the crown since childhood, said clearly that it should go to Sera, and Torren agreed with a rueful grin and a bow. Sera felt dizzy, for she had never wanted to rule a kingdom and only wished that everyone would read the documents more carefully.

Lord Kael, who had followed a bad Chancellor and nearly started a war, said bluntly that the hills would not trust a single ruler again, however honest she might be. Maren Tidewell added in her quiet voice that salt and iron had always depended on each other, and that the two lands wanted a share in the ruling of them both. It was a fair demand, Sera thought, and it was exactly what the Charter had promised in the beginning.

Sera proposed a Council of Salt and Ash, in which the coast, the hills and the Halvane family would each hold equal seats, and every decision about fees and borders would require agreement from all three. She read aloud the old clause that fixed iron and salt weight for weight, and suggested that new scales be cast at the Weigh-Bridge from both metals, so that nobody could ever cheat again. The hall, which had come for a fight and stayed for an argument, broke into loud and surprised applause.

Within a month, smiths from the Ash Hills and glass-workers from the coast were labouring side by side at the Weigh-Bridge, pouring molten iron and clouded salt-glass into the moulds of a pair of great scales. When the new beam was hung, fair and balanced and engraved with the words of the old Charter, the iron carts and the salt wagons began once more to cross the Greywater. People lined both banks to watch, and some of them cheered, and a few of them cried.

Through the long summer and autumn Sera rode back and forth between the coast and the hills, sitting in barns and workshops, listening to miners, farmers and salt-workers and writing down every complaint in a small notebook. The Council met each month, argued fiercely, and settled most of its quarrels with the simple method of reading the Charter aloud. Slowly, like a bruise fading from purple to yellow to nothing, the old resentment between the two lands began to disappear.

In midwinter a ferocious storm drove the sea against the salt pans, and the people of Saltmarch watched the water creep up their wall and feared for their houses and their work. Out of the darkness came a column of carts from Cindermoor, loaded with iron stakes, hammers and shovels, and the miners threw themselves into the mud beside the salt-workers without being asked. By morning the sea wall stood higher than before, and nobody on that coast ever forgot who had built it.

When the spring frosts killed the early crops in the Ash Hills, the miners' families faced the hungry weeks with anxious faces and thin stores. Saltmarch answered with wagons of barrelled fish and sacks of salt for preserving meat, sent without any bargaining, and the miners marvelled at how quickly they had come to depend on their old enemies. Lord Kael was overheard remarking to his daughter that he had never in his life eaten better fish than this.

In the second summer, an envoy from a distant kingdom arrived with a chest of gold and an elegant plan to buy the iron of Cindermoor far below its worth, which would have left the hills poor. Torren charmed the man for three days with dinners and stories until he revealed all that he wanted, and then Lysa, who had waited for exactly that moment, refused him in two firm sentences. The envoy went home with his gold and a deep respect for the Halvanes.

Lysa, who had always believed that a leader should command first and listen afterwards, now spent hours in the miners' halls and salt-workers' cottages, hearing their troubles and asking what they thought. The habit softened her stiff manner and sharpened her judgement, and the soldiers of the Salt Guard began to say that their commander had learned something that no sword could teach. Sera observed these changes with quiet pride and wisely said nothing, for she knew that praise might spoil what patience had grown.

When a year and a day had passed since the old king's death, Master Pell stood in the Hall of Two Crowns and read aloud the final clause of the will, which asked who had kept the peace. Lord Kael stood and said that it was the girl who had walked on the bridge, and Maren Tidewell agreed, and then Lysa and Torren, and then the whole hall in a slow, rising wave. Sera felt the weight of a thousand eyes and wished with all her heart that she could hide in the archive.

Sera opened the old crown case, and beneath the velvet she found a short letter, written in her father's cramped and familiar hand and addressed to no one by name. A crown that is simply handed down, it said, is only a heavy hat, but a crown that is earned can become a bridge between people who would otherwise never meet. She read it twice, folded it carefully, and for the first time in a year felt entirely certain.

Sera accepted the burden of ruling, but she asked that neither crown be placed upon her head, and instead she laid both of them on the table where the Council sat, side by side and equal. For herself she took only a plain ring, forged from the iron of the hills and the glass of the coast, which she wore on her smallest finger where nobody would notice it. The hall, which had expected a glittering coronation, discovered to its own surprise that it much preferred a plain promise.

That evening, in the lamplit quiet of the archive, Sera sat down with Master Pell's second-best pen and began to write the first page of a new chronicle, which she titled simply the Book of the Two Lands. Lysa came in first and then Torren, and the three Halvanes sat together among the old documents, saying very little, while outside the Weigh-Bridge scales swung gently in the night breeze. For the first time since the old king died, there was nothing left to quarrel about, and it was a very good silence.
